title: Duma
full_review:
In Swahili, "zuri" means "beautiful," which makes it the perfect word to describe "Duma" (Warner Bros.), a first-rate coming-of-age story about a boy and his cheetah.

Set against the eye-filling backdrop of southern Africa, the tender tale revolves around a headstrong young Afrikaner named Xan (Alexander Michaletos), who, while driving home with his father (Campbell Scott), happens upon an orphaned cheetah cub, which they name Duma -- the Swahili word for cheetah. They take the animal home to their rural Kenyan ranch. As is common in these types of human-animal buddy films, Xan and Duma quickly develop an unbreakable bond of friendship.

But Xan's happiness is tempered by the unavoidable realization that one day the call of the wild will force a parting of ways.

That day comes sooner than expected, when Xan's father suddenly falls ill and dies, and his mother (an underused Hope Davis) is forced to sell the farm and relocate to the city.

Even Xan realizes that cheetahs do not make ideal apartment pets. So rather than ship Duma off to captivity in a zoo, Xan resolves to return the fleet-footed feline back to his rightful home in the wild, which lies hundreds of miles away, across lion-prowled veldts, crocodile-infested rivers and dense, insect-infested jungles. Worse still, even if they reach their destination safely, Xan worries that Duma has become too domesticated to survive on his own.

With Duma riding shotgun in the sidecar, Xan takes off in his father's motorcycle and into the unknown. Together the two friends battle treacherous terrain, scorching heat, wild animals and inner fears, as Xan's odyssey becomes a journey of self-discovery. Along the way they are aided by Rip (Eamonn Walker), a mysterious drifter whose motives are unclear.

Having grown up in real life on a farm where he raised cheetahs, South African newcomer Michaletos is perfect in the lead role and brings just the right combination of boyish naivete and mature circumspection to the character, making Xan's transformation from rash youth to manhood believable. But the real scene-stealer is Michaletos' sleek and spotted co-star.

Directed by Carroll Ballard, "Duma" combines exceptional nature photography -- including some amazing shots of African wildlife -- with a warm and winning story, resulting in a film that is sweetly charming without being overly sentimental. Ballard is no stranger to adventures involving the pairing of children with animals, having directed films such as "Fly Away Home" and "The Black Stallion."

Loosely based on the fact-based children's book "How It Was With Dooms" by Xan and Carol Cawthra Hopcraft, "Duma" is one of those rare intelligent, well-made films that all but the youngest children can enjoy, one that doesn't need sex or violence -- or, for that matter, flashy special effects -- but is content to tell that most endangered of species: a good story. It should be noted, though, that some images, including the opening scene where Duma's mother is killed by a menacing pride of lions, may be upsetting for some young viewers.

Underneath a plot inspired by "Born Free," the movie deals with difficult issues involving loss, separation, transition and death in a way that is accessible to young viewers. It also imparts a simple but profound message about the permanence of authentic love. As Xan learns, "Love doesn't stop when time passes."

In one scene, Rip tells Xan how, according to local folklore, cheetahs got the distinct black markings cascading down their snouts. He says they were formed by the tears of the first cheetah, who cried after losing her cubs. No doubt, by the movie's bittersweet emotional ending, there may be a few damp human cheeks as well.

The film contains some scenes of peril, and brief wildlife violence which may be frightening to some young children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
